headline: Sea Bright at 5 AM: bluefish choppin' bunker while the bass hide till dark
subhead: The rocks are loud with blues and gulls, but the real striper bite is happening after everyone else goes home.
body_markdown:
Quarter to five, Sea Bright rocks, and there's already a guy out on the third jetty north of the Rumson bridge who beat me there. Again. Older fella, doesn't talk much, throws a white bucktail like it owes him money. We nodded at each other the way you do when you both know the other guy isn't going anywhere. Then the water in front of us just erupted — bunker skying, blues underneath them cutting the school to ribbons, birds dropping out of a still-dark sky like they'd been shot. That's been the show all week from Sea Bright down through Monmouth Beach. Loud, violent, and honestly kind of a relief after how quiet the striper bite's gotten.

We called this one — said last week the bluefish blitz would keep spreading north toward Sandy Hook as long as the bunker stayed pinned along the beach, and that's exactly the picture right now. Every jetty from the Hook down to Monmouth Beach has had at least one morning this week where the water just went white. Poppers are almost unfair right now — a black-and-white Yo-Zuri Hydro Popper or anything that throws spray gets bit on the first cast if you land it inside the bait ball. Metal works too if you want distance — Ava 27s or a 3-ounce Kastmaster, worked fast enough to stay above the blues' teeth. These aren't cocktail blues either. Plenty of 8- to 12-pound choppers mixed in, the kind that'll cut you off if you're running straight mono leader. Sixty-pound fluoro, minimum, or you're re-tying every third fish.

Here's the part that's been humbling: the bass have essentially disappeared during daylight. Water's sitting warm — mid-70s off the beach, and even the deeper holes around the Sea Bright groins aren't holding much heat relief. That pushes stripers onto the thermocline and into nocturnal mode, which is exactly what we flagged happening zone-wide. I fished the Manasquan Inlet rocks three mornings this week at first light and managed one bass — a 26-incher on a 5-inch white Slug-Go, weightless, worked slow along the north jetty face on the last of the outgoing. That fish came at 5:20, right at the edge of usable light. After that, nothing but blues.

The real bass program right now is a night program, and if you're not willing to fish dark water you're going to be frustrated. Shark River Inlet after 10 PM has been the most consistent thing I've heard about or seen myself — the jetty rocks on the north side, working a black Bomber Long A or a bone-colored Gibbs Danny plug on the last two hours of the incoming into the top of high. Slot fish, mostly, 26 to 32 inches, holding tight to the rocks where the current breaks. Nothing epic — two or three fish a tide if you put the time in — but it's real, and it's about the only place bass are eating with any consistency close to shore. Belmar's fishing similarly after dark, same tide window, same idea: current break, dark plug, patience.

Fluke's been the background hum it always is in late July — steady, unspectacular, and exactly what we expected with all this bait keeping things close to the beach. Shark River Inlet channel, drifting bucktails tipped with Gulp in white or chartreuse, 3/4-ounce jigheads working 15 to 20 feet on the deeper edges near the Route 35 bridge, has produced keeper counts in the 2-to-1 short ratio — meaning you're culling through a lot of dinks to find a 19- or 20-incher, but they're there. Same story off Manasquan Inlet's outer edges on the bigger tide swings — fish the last two hours of the ebb when the current's still got some push, because dead slack water in this heat just shuts everything down.

Porgies have been a nice consolation prize for anyone who wants meat in the cooler without babysitting a plug rod all night. The rock piles off Belmar and the pier areas around Spring Lake are loaded with them — squid strips or bloodworms on a high-low rig, small hooks, and you can fill a bucket in an hour on the right tide.

Blackfish are still weeks off — that's an autumn program, not a July one, so don't waste tide time on the wrecks yet.

Looking ahead: I don't see any reason for the bluefish blitz to slow down unless we get a wind shift that scatters the bunker, and there's nothing in the pattern suggesting that happens in the next few days. If you want blitz action, mornings on the Sea Bright-to-Monmouth Beach stretch are the play, and I'd get there before first light because once the sun's up and the joggers show up on the seawall, the bite tends to slide north out of casting range. For bass, I'd commit to a night tide at Shark River or Manasquan — pick the incoming into high, fish it dark, and don't expect volume. Expect quality, and expect to earn it. If the offshore water stays this warm through the week — and there's nothing forecast to cool it down — this nocturnal pattern holds. Plan your trips around dark water, not daylight, and you'll do alright.
